newsitem.title: BELARUS: FORD BOOSTING E. EUROPE PROFILE VIA BELARUS.
newsitem.headline: FORD BOOSTING E. EUROPE PROFILE VIA BELARUS.

text.p: Ford Motor Co , the world's second-largest automaker, plans to boost its presence in eastern Europe next week by opening a vehicle assembly plant in Obchuck, six kilometers northeast of the Belarus capital Minsk.

"This investment will help us to be a major participant in the region," Wayne Booker, Ford vice chairman, told journalists in a telephone conference from his office at Ford headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan.
"You will see a higher profile for Ford in eastern Europe over the next several years -- there's no doubt about that," he added.

The U.S. automaker is launching plans in Belarus with only $9.8 million for a 51 percent stake in a $19.2 million plant with an annual capacity to assemble 6,000 units of Escort cars and Transit vans from imported kits.
But Ford said the venture, named Ford Union (FU), is full of symbolism and potential.

FU's opening ceremony on July 30 will mark the first time that passenger vehicles will be built in Belarus, which became a major manufacturer of agricultural tractors and heavy trucks for the old East bloc.
The Belarus Escorts also will be the first west European cars to be made since the end of communism in the former Soviet Union, where the only foreign brands in production are American and Korean.
"Ford was a pioneer in the region even before the Cold War," Chris Sieder, a Ford media relations official for central and eastern Europe, told Reuters.

"We licensed production of the model 'A' in the 1930s to a plant in Nizhny Novgorod that is now home to GAZ," Seider said, referring to Russia's second-largest automaker, whose full name is AO Gorkovsky Avtomobilny Zavod.

And FU's significance was not lost on the Belarus government, which took a 26 percent stake in the venture by providing $4.0 million in facilities and 11 hectares of land, $1.0 million in cash and a package of tax breaks, Ford said.
The remaining 23 percent of FU is held by Lada-OMC, a Belarus-British joint venture that imports and services Ford vehicles.

The government package includes a five-year exemption on corporate tax profits and an indefinite allowance for duty-free imports of plant equipment and material as well as car bodies and parts that will arrive in kits for assembly at the plant.
"The duty-free import of kits was key to our decision to invest in Belarus," Neil Campbell, FU's general manager, told Reuters.
"It is based on a Ford-specific law that was first established by presidential decree last year," Campbell added. "And it was legislated into effect earlier this month."
But some observers see risks in Ford's advantages, as the company became embroiled in controversy the last time it was granted special treatment for investing in central and eastern Europe.

In the early 1990s, the Hungarian government came under fire from the European Union for a modification in its customs regulations that reduced import duties on commerical vehicles with certain dimensions that applied only to Ford Transits.
The modification, which the government soon rescinded, "blew up in our face," a Ford official in Hungary said at the time.
FU's deal has attracted no heat yet, but Volkswagen AG's Czech automaker Skoda automobilova AS has complained about government obstacles to its own plans to assemble cars in Belarus.
"There have been problems, and we have been waiting for certain political decisions," a Skoda official told Reuters, declining to elaborate.
Recently, though, the Belarus government has softened its stance toward Skoda, which now seems poised to receive similar investment incentives granted to Ford.
And FU said it is confident that its investment is secure.
"The concessions that we received in Belarus are very much in line with efforts by governments world-wide to make industry viable," Campbell of Ford said.
And FU, which has a 99-year rent-free contract to use the land where its plant sits, already envisions expanding onto an adjacent 41 hectares to up its annual output to 200,000 units.
"That's a long way off," Campbell said. "But we have the land for full-scale integrated manufacturing operation here if market demand is sufficient."
The modest beginning in Belarus reflects Ford's conservative approach to central and eastern Europe.

Ford already has invested over $200 million to make auto parts in the Czech Republic and Hungary and vehicles in Poland, but these projects pale against the billions of dollars committed by rivals Daewoo Group, Fiat SPA, General Motors Corp and VW.
The FU project, however, is an important sign that Ford's interest in the region is growing -- and shifting east, Booker said.
Belarus sells only a few thousand new light vehicles a year, and over 80 percent of FU's output is dedicated for Russia, which has an agreement with Belarus for duty-free trade that covers vehicles.
The agreement, which also includes Kazakhstan, has been strained, and Russia has considered imposing a value-added tax on Belarus imports. But observers said they expect duty-free trade to continue.

"The customs union has never worked as intended," Anne Carson, second secretary for the U.S. embassy in Minsk, told journalists visiting Belarus. "I can see it continuing to have problems, but I would be surprised if it falls apart."

Ford officials also said the company wants to supplement exports to Russia with a vehicle assembly plant there, equipped with body and paint shops, that probably would build the small Fiesta and mid-sized Taurus.
"We will invest in Russia -- I'm sure of that," Campbell said. "We're looking at three sites, and a decision could come before 1998. Potentially, the future market in Russia is huge."
